extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of public opinion, political theory, social psychology, and political communication
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and conceptual standards for understanding how individual dispositions, social situations, and political techniques produce collective opinion and homogeneous political behavior. Emphasizes limits of economic and instinctual determinism and the rhetorical/organizational methods by which leaders crystallize public will.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavior as equation of variables
rubrics_metrics.description: The outward behavior of an adult is regarded as an equation between a number of variables, such as the resistance of the environment, repressed cravings of several maturities, and the manifest personality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a multi-variable model when explaining behavior; Kempf's formulation is given (manifest wishes over later repressed wishes over adolescent repressed wishes over preadolescent repressed wishes opposed by environmental resistance = behavior). Do not reduce action to a single cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Situational repression and multiple selves
rubrics_metrics.description: Repression or control of cravings is fixed not in relation to the whole person all the time, but more or less in respect to his various selves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess conduct relative to which 'self' is operative in a situation (e.g., actions taken as a patriot vs. actions taken when not thinking as a patriot). Recognize that buried impulses can be brought to the surface by psychoanalysis or social situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unexpected situations reveal dispositions
rubrics_metrics.description: It is only when our surroundings remain normal and placid ... When the unexpected occurs, we learn much about ourselves that we did not know.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Testories of character should include responses to abnormal or crisis situations (war, disaster) because these reveal dispositions normally suppressed in routine life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selves prescribe appropriate impulses (prepared attitudes)
rubrics_metrics.description: The selves, which we construct with the help of all who influence us, prescribe which impulses, how emphasized, how directed, are appropriate to certain typical situations for which we have learned prepared attitudes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the socially constructed 'self' or role that supplies the prepared attitude; for recognizable types of experience there is a character controlling outward manifestations (example: in civil life murderous hate is controlled; in war the relevant selves change).

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral education must prepare characters for life situations
rubrics_metrics.description: The preparation of characters for all the situations in which men may find themselves is one function of a moral education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral education should either offer patterns of conduct for every phase of life or shield pupils from condemned situations; this requires sincere, knowledgeable exploration of the environment (including economics, politics, psychology) or else each generation will be unprepared for modern complexities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of economic determinism (different situations ≠ fixed opinions)
rubrics_metrics.description: From the existence of differing economic situations you can tentatively infer a probable difference of opinions, but you cannot infer what those opinions will necessarily be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid deterministic inferences that a particular economic position guarantees a specific set of beliefs; economic relations increase probability of certain concerns but do not predict the content or coherence of opinions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for special inquiry to identify causal social relations
rubrics_metrics.description: In trying to explain a certain public opinion, it is rarely obvious which of a man's many social relations is effecting a particular opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When explaining opinion, investigate which specific relation (landlord, employer, consumer, etc.) is salient rather than assuming a single economic cause; empirical/special inquiry is necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class interest is not a single fixed conception
rubrics_metrics.description: A class interest can be conceived largely or narrowly, selfishly or unselfishly, in the light of no facts, some facts, many facts, truth and error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat 'class interest' as monolithic; political mobilization must account for the multiple, competing, and variable ways in which groups conceive their interests—hence socialist prescriptions that assume a single class consciousness are flawed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instincts are reshaped by experience; cognitive/affective aspects matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Every instinctive act in an animal with memory must cease to be 'blind' after being once repeated; instincts become capable of being initiated by ideas and perceptions as well as by natural excitants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for the cognitive and affective components of instinctive processes; only the central part of a disposition remains specific across situations, while the perceptual triggers and bodily movements may be indefinitely complicated by learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variability and attachability of human tendencies
rubrics_metrics.description: All the important tendencies of the creature—appetites, loves, hates, curiosity, sexual cravings, fears, pugnacity—are freely attachable to all sorts of objects as stimulus and gratification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain human behavior by recognizing cultural and historical variability; anthropological evidence supports that stimuli and gratifications differ endlessly across ages and places, undermining claims of fixed human nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public opinion crystallizes despite private variance
rubrics_metrics.description: The living impressions of a large number of people are to an immeasurable degree personal ... How do great numbers of people feeling each so privately about so abstract a picture develop any common will? How are 'the Will of the People' or 'Public Opinion' crystallized out of such fleeting and casual imagery?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek mechanisms (rhetorical, organizational, institutional) by which leaders and campaigns translate heterogeneous private images into a common, actionable public will; do not invoke mystical 'oversoul' explanations when practical technics suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Techniques of political persuasion: binders, ambiguity, and selective emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: Political leaders induce heterogeneous opinion to vote alike by using binders (stereotypes like 'Lincoln'), stretching words to mean all things to all men, selecting opening subjects that avoid explosive conflicts, being specific on neutral facts, and using ambiguous formulas ('American rights') that cover opposing purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating political rhetoric, identify: (a) symbolic binders that transfer reverence, (b) deliberate ambiguity to encompass opposing factions, (c) choice of non-contentious factual narratives to avoid arousing contrary passions, and (d) deliberate obliteration of irreconcilable issues. Examples: Hughes' use of 'Lincoln', his handling of Huerta/Mexico, and the 'American rights' formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electoral outcomes often reflect the least common denominator
rubrics_metrics.description: When there are only two ways of expressing a hundred varieties of feeling, there is no certain way of knowing what the decisive combination was; the least common denominator of all the votes may be the factor that alters policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret election results as aggregations that can mask the multiplicity of motives; policy consequences may diverge from any single voter's motive because the shared minimal factor drove the outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ascribing single motives to mass behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Neither Mr. Harvey nor Mr. Wilson, nor the critics and friends of either, nor any one else, can know quantitatively and qualitatively what went on in thirty or forty million adult minds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious about confidently assigning a unified motive to a population; public action is typically the product of many hybrid motives and cannot be reduced to one speaker's explanation (example: Harvey's rash attributions of 1917 motives).
